Photograph: Jon Nazca/Reuters Social media Russia-linked accounts spread far-right narrative online during Ceuta migration crisis, analysis finds Counter-disinformation group says social media channels connected to Pravda network helped amplify message Aisha Down Fri 7 Aug 2026 12.35 EDT First published on Fri 7 Aug 2026 10.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Accounts with links to the Russian military promoting far-right messages reached more than 500,000 people in the days following the mass influx of people into Ceuta , according to an analysis by 411, a counter-disinformation group. Russia-linked social media accounts frequently spread destabilising narratives in Europe , often promoting far-right talking points about immigration. But 411 and other experts suggest the scale and coordination of the disinformation that followed the Ceuta crisis is significant. Groups spreading disinformation are more organised and powerful than they were several years ago. “We keep seeing this across Europe and we find it very interesting. It seems like there is some type of machinery in place, or structure,” said Saman Nazari, the lead researcher at Alliance4Europe, a Brussels-based nonprofit. “Quite regularly, we are seeing this escalation happening across Europe now, with these types of crises. It is too much of a coincidence to be a bandwagoning effect.” 10:29 How Ceuta migrant crisis exposes divisions within Europe - The Latest The barrage began on 1 August, the day after tens of thousands of people reportedly attempted to cross into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco overnight. This was part of a larger, multi-day crisis during which 72,000 migrants are estimated to have made their way into the small territory in north Africa, the vast majority of whom were swiftly returned. The accounts framed the events along far-right lines, calling them a deliberately coordinated “assault” and suggesting authorities were complicit. Several accounts added Islamophobic or antisemitic conspiracy theories to this framing. These narratives were rapidly reproduced in seven languages and reached more than 720,000 views over the course of six hours on 1 August, according to 411’s examination of roughly 4.5m social media posts. Other far-right accounts called for nationalists to gather in Ceuta and “patrol” businesses and homes, with some apparently coordinating their efforts. Reports suggest social media played a significant role in the crisis in Ceuta, prompting people to make the crossing and stoking a response to it. Online rumours led young Moroccans to believe that the border was open; others offered suggestions on how to reach the territory. The analysis by 411 confirmed reports that there was substantive “peer-to-peer logistics chatter” between potential migrants on social media over how to make the crossing. Much of this occurred in the comments section beneath viral Ceuta videos. This coordination among migrants appeared to be organic, coming “overwhelmingly from small, anonymous-looking individual accounts rather than any single identifiable ‘recruiter’ channel”. A separate, rightwing backlash began on social media as the crossings continued. One origin of the propaganda barrage was Rybar, a Telegram channel with links to Russian intelligence . Rybar’s parent company has faced sanctions in Europe. A network of “repeater” accounts then amplified and spread Rybar’s posts. These included accounts linked to the Pravda network , an operation spreading Kremlin propaganda worldwide. View image in fullscreen Migrant children queue outside a police station to be registered in Ceuta on Thursday. Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters Nazari suggested that disinformation efforts appeared coordinated and that investigations should be made to determine if there were closed forums or similar structures in which far-right influencers discuss how to spread talking points. Ned Mendez, the lead researcher at 411, said disinformation about the Ceuta crisis spread far more quickly than it did in May 2021, during a similar incident in which 8,000 migrants crossed the same border from Morocco into Spain . ‘If we don’t fight back, we don’t have a future’: the journalist taking on the ‘tech fascists’ of Silicon Valley Read more The far right also seized on those events, but this time the amplification of far-right narratives happened more swiftly. The far-right mobilisation calls brought nationalist groups to the main square of Ceuta within days, 411 noted. In 2021, similar calls went out but it took much longer for nationalists to mobilise. “You could compare the process to a highly specific and organised information superhighway,” said Mendez. “If a piece of content or disinformation is placed on to that privileged superhighway, then it will receive a degree of amplification and boost that other types of content just don’t have access to. Events like this across Europe suggest that some pieces of content are being selected for the onramp, and those content pieces share similar characteristics.” The 411 analysis said: “That machinery is the real thing to worry about, more than this particular crisis. The next time there’s a border incident anywhere on the Mediterranean, those same relay networks are already in place, ready to pick it up and run with it again.” Additional reporting by Majida Chowdhury Explore more on these topics Social media Migration The far right Spain Morocco Russia Europe news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Nearly 50 asylum seekers deported under ‘one in one out’ scheme have returned to the UK Nearly a quarter of voters in Europe now back far-right parties Hundreds in Morocco gather near Ceuta border in anxious wait for missing loved ones Anger at ‘send them back’ chants by rightwing MEPs after EU migration law vote France’s top film producer says it will blacklist figures who petitioned against rightwing billionaire EU chief criticises Spain’s migrant plan after Ceuta crisis meeting Stronger EU borders needed after Ceuta crisis, von der Leyen says French film industry at risk from the far right, say actors and directors Ceuta leader accuses Morocco over ‘atrocity’ of mass border crossing Trump lauds Viktor Orbán as Europe’s far-right leaders gather in Budapest Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian Party funding Amendment to bill in Lords could test legality of £72m Reform donations Plans to strengthen legislation already going through parliament might mean donors having to meet stricter UK residence requirements Pippa Crerar , Jessica Elgot and Kiran Stacey Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.01 BST Last modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 21.53 BST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Andy Burnham’s government could thwart Reform’s unprecedented £72m donations with retrospective restrictions on political donors that will include tough new residency requirements, ministers have announced. In a move that is likely to set off furious complaints from Nigel Farage’s party, the government will table amendments to legislation going through the House of Lords within weeks that puts the legality of Reform’s latest donations in doubt. Senior Labour and union figures had urged ministers to look again at party funding rules after Reform announced at the weekend that two cryptocurrency billionaires, Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who have both previously been based overseas, were each donating £36m to the party. Government sources, however, said the plans to strengthen the representation of the people bill had been under way for weeks, after MPs pushed for further action on domestic donations in the House of Commons. Under the proposals, which are expected to be tabled at the Lords committee stage of the legislation, individual donors will have to prove their ongoing physical presence in the UK, in line with the residence requirements applied to other areas of government policy, such as tax status. graphic The extraordinary measure will be seen as a sign of the stakes attached to the donations, which would give Reform a vast advantage in organising supporters on the ground before the next election. However, Farage acknowledged on Monday that Reform could fall foul of government moves to clamp down on foreign donors, although the party has said the £72m donations are in line with both current rules and those already voted on by MPs in the bill. The legislation currently restricts donations from expats to £100,000, which would also apply for the first 12 months after they return to the UK – backdated to 25 March this year. Ministers have already brought in a minimum residency requirement of the remainder of the calendar year in which they return, plus a further full year, meaning Reform may not be able to accept the £72m donations until January 2028. Delo has been based in Hong Kong but said in April he would return to the UK to avoid restrictions, while Harborne was based in Thailand but is believed to have registered to vote in Hampshire in June. “Both these donations are 100% compliant with the law today, of that there is no question whatsoever,” Farage told the BBC. When asked if the two billionaires were UK residents as of 25 March, he replied: “All I’m going to say is, with the law of the land as it stands, they are both compliant.” View image in fullscreen Lady Taylor told peers that the government was considering how it could strengthen the residency requirements of political donors. Photograph: HoL Sharon Taylor, a Labour minister in the Lords, told peers that as well as donors having to demonstrate a “genuine and ongoing connection to the UK”, the government was also looking at further restrictions. “We are considering how we will strengthen the residency requirements, including ensuring the length of time spent in the UK aligns with broader government policy,” Lady Taylor added. Angela Rayner, speaking at the TUC, criticised Reform for suggesting its donations from cryptocurrency billionaires were equivalent to the contributions from trade union members to Labour. “How dare they try to compare money from a couple of crypto billionaires to union members’ subs? The most highly regulated political funding we can have,” the communities secretary said. “It couldn’t be more different from a couple of offshore billionaires trying to buy our democracy … We will never undermine the rights of working people to organise collectively and democratically.” Trade unions are set to issue a statement on Tuesday on political donations condemning attempts by Farage to compare wealthy individual donors with individual members who donate to Labour through their union, and urging the government to go further on political donations. The head of Britain’s union movement, Paul Nowak, said the government must act to “stop the super-rich corrupting our politics”. But union sources had said there were “significant differences” between general secretaries on how to proceed. Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, on Sunday broke ranks and backed a limit on individual domestic donations. But others, including GMB chief Gary Smith, fear it would lead a future rightwing government to curb union donations. Government sources said that calls from opposition parties for any changes to domestic donations to apply to the unions too were “not under active consideration”. However, the government is understood to be looking at spending limits for parties, which are currently restricted to the year before a general election, with tighter limits in the weeks running up to polling day. In a letter to the Electoral Commission in August, Rayner and Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, wrote: “We believe spending limits on parties and candidates are too high, and ought to be reduced.” The government has also set up a cross-government “task and finish” team to consider threats to UK democracy, including political finance, illegitimate influence, and broader threats to political equality. Philip Rycroft, who produced an independent report on tightening electoral law around overseas donations, said the Reform donations reopened broader questions about donations and spending caps. “The time has come when this does need a hard look. It would have been better if the government had started out before we had these huge donations coming down the track,” he said. “But we have to ask the question, is this healthy for our democratic process to have more money coming from fewer people in bigger lumps?” MPs who have campaigned for a donations cap are working with peers on a number of amendments to the bill which would tighten it up without having to wait for another act of parliament. They include one to enable ministers to set a cap on all donations at a later date, and another to prevent spending limits being raised without Electoral Commission approval. Teresa O’Neill, a shadow local government minister in the Lords, said some of the measures in the bill were deeply troubling. “Even just the perception of partisan, targeted legislation risks breaking down longstanding political conventions and, crucially, trust in the system,” she said. Reform denounced the government’s existing plans, with Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, describing them on X as “an unprecedented step from a leftwing government to plunge Britain into dictatorship and communism”. https://praguemonitor.com/pm/czechia/cha.text: Czechia Business Prague Housing Europe & World Work & Life Briefings Key points Charles IV, born in Prague in 1316, was King of Bohemia from 1346 and Holy Roman Emperor from 1355, and he made Prague an imperial capital. In his reign Prague gained an archbishopric (1344), a university (1348), the New Town (1348) and the foundations of St Vitus Cathedral and the stone bridge now named after him. His reign is called the Golden Age of the Czech lands, a label that celebrates real achievements and also simplifies a more complicated record. On this page 6 sections A king born in Prague, raised abroad Why Prague What he built The wider kingdom A Golden Age, with qualifications What survives, and how to see it Take a walk from the Old Town to the Castle and almost every landmark on the way has the same sponsor. The stone bridge, the Gothic cathedral on the hill, the university building you pass in the lanes, even the layout of the streets south of Wenceslas Square owe something to one man who ruled in the fourteenth century. Czechs call him Otec vlasti , father of the fatherland, and have printed his face on the 100-koruna note. Understanding Charles IV is a shortcut to understanding why Prague looks the way it does. This is a history explainer, written for residents and visitors who want the story behind the stones. Dates are those commonly given in standard histories; for the buildings, the Prague Castle and city sites are the best primary sources. A king born in Prague, raised abroad Charles was born in Prague on 14 May 1316 and christened Wenceslas, after the national patron. His father was John of Luxembourg, King of Bohemia, a restless knight-king who spent more time abroad than at home. His mother was Elizabeth, a Přemyslid, the last family line of the old Bohemian dynasty, which gave Charles a direct link to the saints and rulers of the earlier kingdom. Our piece on the Přemyslids tells that earlier story. At seven he was sent to the French court, where he took the name Charles at his confirmation, in honour of the French king. He learned several languages, and later wrote a Latin autobiography, the Vita Caroli , which survives. In his twenties he governed Moravia as margrave and spent time in Italy, learning how a state is run. When his father died at the Battle of Crécy in 1346, Charles became King of Bohemia, and in that same year he had already been elected King of the Romans with the support of the pope. In numbers year Charles IV was born in Prague 1316 year he was crowned Holy Roman Emperor in Rome 1355 year the historic centre of Prague was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List 1992 Source: Prague Castle; UNESCO World Heritage Centre Why Prague Charles did something unusual for a medieval emperor: he chose a capital and stayed in it. The Holy Roman Empire had no fixed seat, and emperors travelled from court to court. Charles made Prague his main residence and the centre of imperial government, and he spent money and political energy to match. The decision reflected a plain calculation. Bohemia was the richest and most secure territory he held, and its king was one of the electors who chose the emperor. The Golden Bull of 1356, the imperial law that fixed how emperors were chosen, confirmed the king of Bohemia as the senior secular elector. So his Prague was a political project. A capital needs a church hierarchy, a university, a defended city, courtly buildings and a population. He built or founded all of them. What he built The archbishopric, 1344. Charles secured the elevation of Prague from a bishopric under Mainz to an archbishopric. This gave Bohemia its own church head and made Prague a major ecclesiastical seat. St Vitus Cathedral, 1344. The foundation stone of a new Gothic cathedral was laid in 1344 on the Castle hill. The French architect Matthias of Arras began it, and after his death the young Peter Parler, from Swabia, took over in 1356. Parler's workshop shaped much of the Prague Gothic. The cathedral was finished only in the twentieth century. Charles University, 1348. Founded by royal charter on 7 April 1348, it was among the first universities in Central Europe. It brought scholars from across the Empire and trained the Czech elite. Our piece on the Hussite movement shows how the university's masters later shaped events. The New Town, 1348. On 8 March 1348 Charles founded a new city adjoining the Old Town, planned on a large scale with broad streets and three great markets. Those markets survive as Wenceslas Square (once the horse market), Charles Square (the cattle market) and the Senovážné square (the hay market). Seen from above, the grid is the clearest sign that Prague was planned, not just grown. The bridge, from 1357. After floods destroyed the earlier Judith Bridge in 1342, a new stone crossing was begun in 1357. Tradition says the foundation stone was laid on 9 July at 5:31 in the morning, so that the numbers 1357 9 7 5 31 read the same forwards and backwards. Whether or not the story is true, the bridge stood for centuries, and its Gothic tower at the Old Town end is Parler's work. The row of statues is much later, from the Baroque period. Karlštejn Castle, from 1348. Built in the hills southwest of Prague to hold the imperial regalia and relics. It lies outside the city but belongs to the same plan. The Hunger Wall. The fortification that still climbs Petřín hill dates from Charles's reign, built in the 1360s to defend the New Town. The nickname comes from a later legend about it being a make-work project in a hungry year. Charles IV in dates 1316 Born in Prague, christened Wenceslas 1344 Prague raised to an archbishopric; foundation stone of St Vitus Cathedral 1346 Elected King of the Romans; becomes King of Bohemia after his father dies at Crécy 1348 Founds Charles University and the New Town; begins Karlštejn 1355 Crowned Holy Roman Emperor in Rome 1356 Golden Bull confirms the king of Bohemia as an imperial elector 1357 Work begins on the stone bridge 1378 Dies in Prague on 29 November The wider kingdom Charles also tried to bind the Czech lands into a single legal unit. He developed the idea of the Crown of the Bohemian Lands, in which Bohemia, Moravia, Silesia and Lusatia were seen as belonging to the Crown of St Wenceslas, not to the person of the king. A crown of St Wenceslas was made for his coronation in 1347, and it is still among the Czech Crown Jewels, kept in the cathedral. The concept of a continuous Bohemian Crown shaped the politics of the region for centuries. He supported trade, set up mints and generally encouraged the growth of towns. Prague became one of the larger cities of Central Europe by the standards of the time, a magnet for builders, scholars, merchants and artists, many from German lands and further afield. The city was multilingual: Czech, German and Latin were all in daily use. A Golden Age, with qualifications The phrase "Golden Age" is old and affectionate, and it has a reason. Charles's reign did bring peace and growth to Bohemia, and it left a built legacy that the city still lives on. But historians point out limits. The Black Death passed through Europe in his time. Prosperity was uneven, and the tax burden on towns and the countryside was real. Charles was a pious ruler and a political realist who bought support, arranged marriages and used the Church as an instrument of government. His son and successor Wenceslas IV inherited a kingdom with tensions that his father had managed and he could not. The era also left an unresolved legacy: wealthy bishoprics, a reform-minded university and a lively debate about the Church. Within a generation Prague was the centre of the movement that followed Jan Hus. Walk it in an afternoon Start at the Old Town Bridge Tower, cross the Charles Bridge, climb to the Castle and St Vitus Cathedral, then come back to the Charles Square on the New Town side. You will cover the main works of one reign in a few hours. What survives, and how to see it The Historic Centre of Prague was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1992, and Charles's works are central to the listing. St Vitus Cathedral and the Charles Bridge are open to the public, though opening hours and ticket arrangements change, so check the Prague Castle and city websites. The Old Town Bridge Tower can be climbed. Karlštejn is reached by a train from Prague's main railway station in under an hour, and tickets and tour rules are on its official site. For present-day readers, the legacy runs through the university, which is still Czechia's oldest and largest, and through the street plan of the New Town. How the city is run today is explained in how Prague is governed , and the longer sweep of the story is in our short history of Czechia . Frequently asked questions Why is Charles IV called the father of the fatherland? The title Otec vlasti was applied to him after his death, in recognition of the prosperity and prestige he brought to the Czech lands. Did Charles IV build the Charles Bridge? He ordered it, and construction began in 1357 under his rule. It was completed after his death, and the name 'Charles Bridge' was applied later. Is Charles University the oldest in Central Europe? It was founded in 1348 and is among the oldest universities in the region, and the oldest in Czechia. Was Charles IV Czech? He was born in Prague to a Luxembourg father and a Přemyslid mother, spoke Czech among several languages, and ruled the Empire as well as Bohemia.
